phy_ocrb.1.0.summary: An electric current is a flow of charge that **transfers energy** from a source (cell, battery or mains supply) to the components in a circuit, where the energy is shifted into other stores such as thermal stores, or carried away by light and sound. **Power** is the **rate of energy transfer**, measured in **watts** (1 W = 1 J/s), and an appliance's **power rating** tells you how much energy it transfers each second. The energy transferred is found from **energy transferred = power x time**, measured in **joules** (power in W, time in s) or in **kilowatt-hours** (power in kW, time in h), and the kWh is the unit used on electricity bills to work out cost.

core.h: Energy transfer by an electric current
core.p: A circuit is a way of moving energy from one place to another. The **cell or supply** pushes charge round the circuit; as the current flows through components, it **transfers energy** to them. We say the energy is transferred **electrically** (by an electric current, sometimes called **electrical working**).
bullets: In a battery-powered torch, energy is transferred from the **chemical store** of the battery, electrically, to the lamp.
The lamp transfers energy by **light** (radiation) to the surroundings and to its own and the surroundings' **thermal stores**.
In a mains-powered kettle, energy is transferred electrically from the power station, via the National Grid, to the **thermal store** of the water.
In an electric motor, energy is transferred electrically to the **kinetic store** of the moving parts.
Wires do not 'store' electricity: the current is the means of transfer, not a store.
Energy is always **conserved**: the total transferred out of the supply equals the total transferred into other stores, though some is usually wasted (dissipated) as heating.

callouts.p: Electricity is a **pathway** (energy transferred electrically), not an energy store.

core.p: Each appliance is designed to transfer energy into a particular useful store, but there is usually some wasted transfer as well.
bullets: Start from the **supply**: chemical store (battery) or the mains (energy from a power station).
The pathway is always **electrical** (by the current).
End with the **useful store or pathway** the appliance is designed for, then name the **wasted** transfer.
Almost every appliance wastes some energy by heating its surroundings, because current heats wires and components.

core.h: Power: the rate of energy transfer
core.p: **Power** tells you how **quickly** energy is transferred. Two appliances can transfer the same total energy, but the one with the higher power does it in less time.
bullets: Power is measured in **watts (W)**.
**1 watt = 1 joule per second** (1 W = 1 J/s).
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W; 1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W.
A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J of energy every second.
A higher-power kettle boils the same water faster because it transfers energy at a greater rate.
Power = energy transferred / time, which is the same equation as energy = power x time rearranged.

callouts.p: Power is the **rate of energy transfer**: the energy transferred per second.

core.p: The **power rating** of an appliance, printed on it, is the rate at which it transfers energy when it is working normally at its intended voltage.
bullets: Appliances that heat things (kettles, heaters, showers, ovens) generally have the **highest** power ratings, of a few kilowatts.
Appliances that produce light or process information (LED lamps, phone chargers, laptops) have **low** power ratings.
Replacing a filament lamp (about 60 W) with an LED lamp (about 6 to 10 W) giving similar light reduces the energy used.
A higher power rating does not mean an appliance is better or more efficient; it just transfers energy faster.
How much energy an appliance uses depends on **both** its power and **how long** it is switched on.

callouts.p: To compare appliances quickly, compare power ratings. To compare **total** energy used, multiply power by time for each.

core.p: If power is energy per second, the total energy transferred is the power multiplied by the number of seconds. This equation must be recalled and applied.
bullets: **energy transferred (J) = power (W) x time (s)**.
In symbols: E = P x t.
Rearranged: P = E / t and t = E / P.
Time must be in **seconds** when using watts and joules: 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s.
Energy can be large: a 2 kW heater on for one hour transfers 2000 x 3600 = 7 200 000 J (7.2 MJ).
Because joules are tiny on a household scale, a bigger unit, the kilowatt-hour, is used for bills.

callouts.p: energy transferred = power x time

core.p: A **kilowatt-hour** is the energy transferred by a **1 kW appliance in 1 hour**. It is a unit of **energy**, not power.
bullets: **energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h)**.
To use kWh, power must be in **kilowatts** and time in **hours**.
Electricity meters record energy used in kWh, often called 'units' of electricity.
Examples: a 3 kW kettle on for 0.1 h uses 0.3 kWh; a 10 W LED on for 100 h uses 1 kWh.

callouts.p: The kilowatt-hour is a unit of **energy**. Do not confuse it with the kilowatt, which is a unit of **power**.

core.p: Exam questions often mix units. Choose one consistent set before calculating.
bullets: W and s give J. kW and h give kWh.
kWh to J: multiply by 3 600 000.
J to kWh: divide by 3 600 000.
W to kW: divide by 1000. Minutes to hours: divide by 60.
Check your answer is sensible: household energy per day is typically a few kWh to tens of kWh.

core.p: Suppliers charge for each kilowatt-hour transferred. The cost depends on the power, the time and the price per unit.
bullets: **cost = energy transferred (kWh) x price per kWh**.
So cost = power (kW) x time (h) x price per kWh.
Meter method: units used = later reading - earlier reading; then multiply by price per kWh.
Prices are often given in pence per kWh; convert to pounds by dividing by 100 if asked.
Reducing cost: use lower power appliances (LED lamps), use appliances for less time, and choose more efficient devices.

callouts.p: Write units at each step (kW, h, kWh, p) and you are much less likely to slip.

core.h: Why heating appliances have high power
core.p: Heating water or a room needs a large amount of energy, and we want it done quickly, so heating appliances need high power ratings.
bullets: Warming 1 kg of water by 1 degree C needs about 4200 J, so boiling a kettle needs hundreds of thousands of joules.
To do that in a few minutes requires a power of a few thousand watts.
Electric showers can be 8 to 10 kW because they must heat flowing water instantly.
This is why the biggest savings on bills usually come from heating appliances, not lamps or chargers.

core.h: Comparing appliances: power versus total energy
core.p: A high power appliance used briefly can use less energy than a low power appliance left on for a long time. Always multiply power by time before comparing.
bullets: 3 kW kettle for 3 minutes (0.05 h): 0.15 kWh.
100 W TV for 4 hours: 0.1 kW x 4 h = 0.4 kWh.
So the TV uses more energy in the evening than the kettle, despite its much lower power.
Standby mode: a few watts left on for 24 hours a day all year adds up to many kWh.

core.h: Electrical link: power, current and voltage
core.p: In the electricity chapter you will also meet the link between power, current and potential difference. It explains why higher-power appliances draw larger currents from the mains.
bullets: power (W) = potential difference (V) x current (A).
On a 230 V mains supply, a 2300 W kettle draws a current of 10 A, while a 23 W lamp draws only 0.1 A.
This is why high-power appliances need thicker cables and higher-rated fuses.

analogy.p: Think of energy as water and the power rating as how far the tap is turned on: litres per second is like joules per second (watts). The total water in the bath is the power multiplied by how long the tap runs, just like energy = power x time. A kilowatt-hour is like measuring the water in big buckets instead of teaspoons, so the numbers on the bill are manageable. Where it breaks down: the energy is not stored in the appliance like water in a bath; it is transferred onward to other stores (mostly thermal) and spreads out into the surroundings.

phy_ocrb.1.1.summary: Energy is **conserved**: it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between **stores**, so the total energy before any change equals the total energy after. In every real process some energy is **dissipated**, meaning it spreads out into the surroundings (usually by heating them) and becomes less useful. We can **reduce unwanted energy transfers** by **lubrication** (reducing friction) and by **thermal insulation**, which uses materials with **low thermal conductivity**, often trapping air, to reduce the rate of energy transfer by heating, for example in homes with loft and cavity wall insulation and double glazing.

core.p: To describe any energy change, identify the **stores** that energy moves from and to, and the **pathway** by which it is transferred.
bullets: **Stores**: chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal (internal), magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear.
**Pathways (ways of transferring)**: mechanically (by a force moving), electrically (by a current), by heating (because of a temperature difference), by radiation (light, infrared, sound waves).
Example: a falling ball transfers energy from its gravitational potential store to its kinetic store, mechanically (by the force of gravity).
Example: a kettle transfers energy electrically to the thermal store of the water.
Describing the start and end stores is often enough for marks; you do not need to list every step.

core.p: The **principle of conservation of energy** is one of the most important laws in physics. It applies to every situation, including those where energy seems to 'disappear'.
bullets: Energy **cannot be created or destroyed**, only transferred from one store to another (or stored).
So, in a closed system, **total energy in = total energy out**.
This lets you calculate a missing energy value: useful energy + wasted energy = total energy supplied.
When a swing slows down, the energy has not vanished; it has been transferred to the thermal stores of the air and the pivot.
Energy 'used up' really means energy transferred to stores where we cannot use it.

callouts.p: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but **cannot be created or destroyed**.

core.p: In every real energy transfer, some energy is transferred to stores where it is not useful. This is called **dissipation**: the energy **spreads out** into the surroundings, usually raising their temperature very slightly.
bullets: Dissipated energy usually ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
It is spread so thinly (a tiny temperature rise in a large amount of air) that it is very hard to use again.
Causes include **friction** between moving parts, **air resistance**, **electrical resistance** in wires (current heats them) and **sound**.
Sound energy is also eventually absorbed and heats the surroundings.
The more energy dissipated, the less is transferred usefully, so the lower the efficiency.
Dissipation is why no machine can keep going forever without an energy supply (no perpetual motion).

callouts.p: Wasted energy is still there, it is just **dissipated** (spread out) to the surroundings, often by heating.

fig.cap: A swinging pendulum transfers energy back and forth between its gravitational potential and kinetic stores. Air resistance and friction at the pivot dissipate some energy to the thermal store of the surroundings each swing, so the swing gets smaller.

core.p: Engineers try to reduce dissipation so that more of the input energy is transferred usefully.
bullets: **Lubrication**: oil or grease between moving parts reduces **friction**, so less energy is transferred to thermal stores (for example oiling a bicycle chain or engine).
**Streamlining**: shaping cars, trains and aircraft to reduce **air resistance** (drag).
Using **low-resistance wires** (thicker cables) to reduce heating in electrical circuits.
Fitting bearings so parts roll instead of sliding.
Tightening loose parts to reduce vibration and sound.
Replacing inefficient devices, such as filament lamps with LEDs, which waste far less energy by heating.

core.p: When there is a temperature difference, energy is transferred from the hotter region to the colder one. In solids this happens mainly by **conduction**.
bullets: In conduction, particles in the hotter part vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles through collisions.
In metals, free electrons also carry energy quickly through the material, so metals are good conductors.
Gases are poor conductors because their particles are far apart, so collisions are less frequent.
Energy also leaves buildings by **convection** (warm air rising and moving) and by **radiation** (infrared emitted from warm surfaces).
The **bigger the temperature difference**, the faster the rate of energy transfer.

core.p: **Thermal conductivity** describes how well a material conducts energy by heating. Materials with **high** thermal conductivity transfer energy quickly; those with **low** thermal conductivity are **thermal insulators**.
bullets: The **higher the thermal conductivity**, the **higher the rate** of energy transfer by conduction through the material.
Metals (copper, aluminium) have high thermal conductivity: used for saucepan bases and heat sinks.
Air, foam, wool, fibreglass and plastic have low thermal conductivity: used as insulators.
Many insulators work by **trapping air** in small pockets, which also stops convection currents.
The rate of energy transfer through a wall also depends on its **thickness** (thicker = slower) and its **area** (bigger = faster), and on the temperature difference.

callouts.p: Lower thermal conductivity, thicker walls, smaller area and a smaller temperature difference all give a **lower rate of energy transfer**.

core.p: Heating a home costs money and uses energy resources. Keeping the energy in for longer means the heating needs to supply less energy to keep the house warm.
bullets: **Loft insulation**: thick layers of fibreglass or mineral wool trap air, reducing conduction and convection through the roof.
**Cavity wall insulation**: foam or fibres injected into the gap between the two brick walls trap air and stop convection currents in the cavity.
**Double glazing**: two panes of glass with a gap of air or argon between; the gas is a poor conductor, reducing conduction.
**Draught excluders**: strips around doors and windows reduce convection (warm air escaping, cold air entering).
**Thick walls** and walls made of low thermal conductivity materials reduce the rate of conduction.
**Carpets and underfloor insulation** reduce energy transfer through the floor.
**Reflective foil** behind radiators reflects infrared back into the room.

callouts.p: For each measure, say **what** it reduces (conduction, convection or radiation) and **why** (traps air, low thermal conductivity, reflects infrared).

core.p: Insulation costs money to install but saves money on heating each year. Comparing measures uses the **payback time**.
bullets: **payback time = installation cost / annual saving**.
Loft insulation is usually cheap and has a short payback time.
Double glazing is expensive and has a long payback time, although it also reduces noise and condensation.
Cheapest measures (draught excluders) can have payback times of under a year.
Wider benefits: less fuel burned, so less carbon dioxide emitted.

callouts.p: The **shortest** payback time is the most cost-effective. Example numbers vary; always use the data given in the question.

core.p: A common practical investigation compares how well different materials insulate a beaker of hot water, by measuring how quickly it cools.
bullets: Wrap identical beakers in different materials (or different thicknesses of one material); keep one unwrapped as a control.
Pour the **same volume** of hot water at the **same starting temperature** into each beaker and fit a lid.
Record the temperature with a thermometer every minute for 10 to 20 minutes.
Plot temperature against time: the best insulator gives the **shallowest curve** (smallest temperature drop).
Control variables: volume of water, starting temperature, room temperature, beaker type, thickness of material, lid.
Cooling is fastest at first because the temperature difference with the room is largest.

callouts.p: Change only one independent variable (the material or the thickness) and measure the temperature drop in a fixed time.

core.p: Whether energy transferred by heating is wasted depends on the purpose of the device.
bullets: In a kettle or heater, heating is the **useful** transfer.
In a lamp, motor or phone, heating is **wasted** (dissipated) energy.
Sometimes wasted energy can be **recovered**: car engines heat the passenger compartment; power stations can use waste heat for district heating.
Keeping a hot drink in a vacuum flask reduces unwanted transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.

core.h: Writing long answers on energy saving
core.p: Six mark questions often ask you to evaluate ways of reducing energy loss from a home or device. Combine physics explanations with use of data.
bullets: Identify where most energy is lost (use the data).
Explain how each measure reduces the rate of energy transfer (mechanism and material property).
Compare cost, saving and payback time.
Reach a justified conclusion, for example 'loft insulation first because it has the shortest payback time'.
Mention conservation: the energy is not destroyed, it is dissipated to the surroundings.

analogy.t: Money in a bank and leaky pockets
analogy.p: Think of energy as money that can move between accounts (stores) but can never be printed or destroyed: the total always stays the same. Dissipation is like loose change falling through holes in your pockets and scattering across a huge field: it still exists, but it is spread so thinly you can never usefully gather it back. Lubrication and insulation are like sewing up the holes so less escapes. Where it breaks down: lost coins keep their value, but dissipated energy really does become less useful because it is spread out at a low temperature, not just hard to find.

terms.d: A way in which energy is held, for example kinetic, chemical, thermal or gravitational potential.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, stored or dissipated.
A system where no energy enters or leaves, so the total energy stays constant.
When energy spreads out into the surroundings, usually by heating, so it becomes less useful.
Energy transferred to stores that are not useful for the intended purpose.
Energy transferred to the store or by the pathway that the device is designed for.
A force between surfaces that opposes motion and transfers energy to thermal stores.
Using oil or grease between moving surfaces to reduce friction and so reduce unwanted energy transfer.
Transfer of energy through a material by particle vibrations and collisions (and free electrons in metals).
Transfer of energy by the movement of a warmer fluid (liquid or gas) carrying energy with it.
A measure of how quickly a material transfers energy by conduction; the higher it is, the higher the rate of transfer.
A material with low thermal conductivity that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
Foam or fibres placed in the gap between two walls to trap air and stop convection.
Windows with two panes of glass separated by a gap of air or argon to reduce conduction.
Installation cost divided by the annual saving; the time taken for savings to cover the cost.

mistakes.w: Energy is used up / lost / destroyed.
mistakes.r: Energy is **conserved**; it is **transferred** or **dissipated** to the surroundings, not destroyed.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops heat escaping completely.
mistakes.r: Insulation **reduces the rate** of energy transfer; it does not stop it.

mistakes.w: Double glazing works because glass is a good insulator.
mistakes.r: It works mainly because the **gap of air or argon** has very low thermal conductivity.

mistakes.w: Cavity wall insulation works because foam is a solid.
mistakes.r: Foam **traps air** in small pockets, which reduces conduction and stops **convection** in the cavity.

mistakes.w: Insulation keeps the cold out.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from **hot to cold**; insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer **out** of the warm house.

mistakes.w: Lubrication removes friction.
mistakes.r: Lubrication **reduces** friction, so less energy is **dissipated** by heating.

mistakes.w: A material with high thermal conductivity is a good insulator.
mistakes.r: Good insulators have **low** thermal conductivity.

mistakes.w: The best insulation measure is the one that saves the most money per year.
mistakes.r: Cost-effectiveness depends on **payback time** (cost / annual saving), not saving alone.

exam.q: State the principle of conservation of energy.
model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred (stored or dissipated)

exam.q: What is meant by energy being dissipated?
model: Energy spreads out to the surroundings (usually heating them) and becomes less useful

exam.q: Explain why oiling a bicycle chain makes cycling easier.
model: Oil reduces friction between moving parts
So less energy is dissipated to thermal stores, more transferred to kinetic store
exam.tip: Link lubrication to friction to wasted energy.

exam.q: Explain how double glazing reduces energy transfer from a house.
model: Gap between panes contains air/argon (or vacuum)
Gas has low thermal conductivity so reduces conduction through the window
exam.tip: Focus on the gap, not the glass.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 350 J to the kinetic store of a load. Calculate the energy dissipated.
model: Energy dissipated = 500 - 350

exam.q: Describe how the thickness and thermal conductivity of a wall affect the rate of energy transfer through it.
model: Thicker wall gives a lower rate of energy transfer
Lower thermal conductivity gives a lower rate of energy transfer

exam.q: Loft insulation costs 450 pounds and saves 150 pounds per year. Calculate the payback time.
model: Payback = 450 / 150
= 3 years

exam.q: A ball is dropped and each bounce is lower than the last. Explain this in terms of energy.
model: Energy transferred between gravitational potential, kinetic and elastic stores
Some energy dissipated each bounce by air resistance, sound and heating of ball/floor
So less energy in gravitational potential store at top of each bounce; total energy is conserved

exam.q: Describe an experiment to compare how well three materials work as thermal insulators.
model: Wrap identical beakers in each material, with an unwrapped control
Same volume of hot water at the same starting temperature in each
Same thickness of material and a lid on each
Measure temperature with a thermometer at regular intervals (e.g. every minute for 10 minutes)
Calculate temperature drop or plot cooling curves
Material with smallest temperature drop / shallowest curve is the best insulator
exam.tip: Level 3: clear method, named control variables and how the results are used to reach a conclusion.

exam.q: A homeowner can afford one of cavity wall insulation (cost 600 pounds, saves 150 pounds per year) or double glazing (cost 3600 pounds, saves 90 pounds per year). Evaluate which they should choose.
model: Cavity wall payback = 600 / 150 = 4 years
Double glazing payback = 3600 / 90 = 40 years
Cavity wall insulation is more cost-effective (and saves more per year)
Double glazing may have other benefits, such as noise reduction

exam.q: Explain why cooling of a cup of tea is fastest at the start.
model: Temperature difference between tea and room is largest at the start
Rate of energy transfer is greater when the temperature difference is greater

worked.q: An electric fan is supplied with 1200 J. 900 J is transferred to the kinetic store of the air, and 100 J is transferred as sound. How much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the motor and surroundings?
steps: Conservation of energy: total in = total out.
worked.ans: 200 J is dissipated by heating (and the 100 J of sound is eventually dissipated as well).

worked.q: A family's heating bill is 1200 pounds per year. Loft insulation (cost 500 pounds) reduces energy loss through the roof, which accounts for 25% of the loss, by two thirds. Estimate the payback time.
steps: Cost of energy lost through roof = 25% of 1200 = 300 pounds per year.
Saving = two thirds of 300 = 200 pounds per year.

worked.q: In an insulation experiment, water in beaker A cools from 80 C to 62 C in 10 minutes, and in beaker B (wrapped in wool) from 80 C to 71 C. Compare the materials.
steps: B lost half the temperature, so the rate of energy transfer was lower.
Wool has lower thermal conductivity and traps air.
worked.ans: The wool is the better insulator: it halved the temperature drop in the same time.

phy_ocrb.1.2.summary: No real device transfers all of its input energy usefully: some is always dissipated, usually by heating the surroundings. **Efficiency** tells you what fraction of the input energy ends up where you want it, and is calculated as useful energy transferred divided by total energy supplied (or useful power output divided by total power input). **Sankey diagrams** show the same story as a picture, with arrow widths drawn to scale so you can read off and compare useful and wasted energy at a glance.

core.p: Efficiency compares the energy a device transfers usefully with the total energy you put into it. Because energy is conserved, the input energy must equal the useful output plus the wasted output, so the useful part can never be more than the input.
bullets: **Useful energy** is energy transferred to the store or by the pathway you want (for example the kinetic store of a motor, or light from a lamp).
**Wasted energy** is energy transferred to stores you do not want, almost always the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
Wasted energy is **dissipated**: it spreads out into the surroundings and becomes less useful, but it is **not destroyed**.
Efficiency has **no units**: it is a ratio of two energies (or two powers).
It can be written as a **decimal** (0 to 1) or a **percentage** (0% to 100%).

callouts.p: Efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy transferred (multiply by 100 for a percentage).

core.p: OCR expects you to recall and use this equation, and to rearrange it to find the useful energy or the input energy.
bullets: efficiency = useful energy transferred (J) / total energy transferred (J)
percentage efficiency = (useful energy transferred / total energy transferred) x 100%
Rearranged: useful energy = efficiency x total energy (use efficiency as a decimal).
Rearranged: total energy = useful energy / efficiency.
Both energies must be in the **same unit** (both J, both kJ or both kWh) so the units cancel.
**Total energy transferred** means the input energy supplied to the device, not the wasted energy.

callouts.p: When rearranging, convert a percentage to a decimal first (35% = 0.35). Dividing by 35 instead of 0.35 is a common way to lose the mark.

core.p: Power is energy transferred per second, so in a fixed time the ratio of powers is the same as the ratio of energies. This lets you calculate efficiency straight from power ratings.
bullets: efficiency = useful power output (W) / total power input (W)
Works because energy = power x time, and the time cancels top and bottom.
Example: a motor with 400 W input and 300 W useful output has efficiency 300 / 400 = 0.75 = 75%.
Wasted power = input power - useful output power (here 100 W).
Use this version whenever the question gives watts rather than joules.

callouts.p: Energy efficiency and power efficiency always give the same answer for the same device over the same time.

core.p: The principle of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed. A device cannot output more useful energy than it receives, so an efficiency above 1 (or 100%) means a calculation mistake.
bullets: Every real device has some **friction**, **electrical resistance** or **air resistance**, which dissipate energy by heating.
So every real device has efficiency **less than 100%**.
An answer such as 125% almost always means useful and total have been put the wrong way round.
Electric heaters are a special case: the 'wasted' heat is the useful output, so they are very close to 100% efficient.

callouts.p: If you get an efficiency greater than 1 or 100%, you have divided the wrong way. Swap the numbers.

core.p: A Sankey diagram is a flow diagram for energy. The input arrow splits into output arrows, and the **width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy** it represents.
bullets: The input arrow enters from the **left**.
The **useful** output usually continues **straight on** to the right.
**Wasted** outputs usually bend **downwards** (or upwards) away from the main flow.
Widths add up: width of input = sum of widths of all outputs (conservation of energy).
Each arrow should be **labelled** with the type of energy transfer and its value in joules (or per second, in watts).
Diagrams are usually drawn on **squared paper** with a scale, for example 1 small square = 10 J.

callouts.p: A diagram showing energy transfers in which the width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy transferred.

core.h: Reading values from a Sankey diagram
core.p: To read a Sankey diagram you count squares or measure widths using the scale, then use the values in the efficiency equation.
bullets: Step 1: work out the **scale** (energy per square or per mm).
Step 2: measure the width of the **input** arrow and of the **useful** arrow.
Step 3: convert widths to energies using the scale.
Step 4: efficiency = useful width / input width (the scale cancels, so you can even use squares directly).
If one output is missing, find it by subtraction: missing = input - other outputs.

callouts.p: Because efficiency is a ratio, useful squares / input squares gives the efficiency without converting to joules.

core.p: Exam questions often give you partly completed squared grids and ask you to finish the diagram. Marks come from correct widths and labels.
bullets: Choose a sensible **scale** so the input arrow fills a good part of the grid.
Draw the input arrow with the correct width.
Split it: useful arrow straight on with the correct width, wasted arrow(s) curving away.
Check widths add up to the input width.
**Label** every arrow with what it is (light, kinetic, heating surroundings, sound) and the energy value.
Use a ruler; arrowheads at the ends of each output.

callouts.p: The energy is shown by the WIDTH of an arrow, not its length. A long thin arrow still represents only a small amount of energy.

core.p: Knowing rough efficiencies helps you judge whether an answer is sensible and lets you compare devices in longer questions.
bullets: Devices that rely on making something very hot (filament lamps, petrol engines) are usually **inefficient**.
Electric motors and transformers are usually **highly efficient**.
LED lamps are much more efficient than filament lamps, which is why they have replaced them.
Thermal power stations are limited because a lot of energy must be dissipated by heating the surroundings (cooling towers).

core.h: Where wasted energy goes and why
core.p: The wasted energy in almost every device ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings. Understanding the mechanism lets you suggest how to reduce it.
bullets: **Friction** between moving parts heats them and the surroundings.
**Electrical resistance** in wires heats them when current flows.
**Air resistance (drag)** transfers energy to the air.
**Sound** is also dissipated and ends up as thermal energy of the surroundings.
Dissipated energy is spread out at a low temperature, so it is very hard to use again.

callouts.p: Say energy is dissipated or wasted to the surroundings. Never say energy is lost or used up, as that contradicts conservation of energy.

core.p: To improve efficiency you reduce the wasted energy so that more of the input is transferred usefully. Each method targets a particular cause of waste.
bullets: **Lubrication** (oil, grease) reduces friction between moving parts.
**Streamlining** reduces air resistance on vehicles.
Using **thicker wires** or lower-resistance materials reduces heating in cables.
**Thermal insulation** reduces unwanted heating of surroundings when you want to keep something hot.
Replacing old technology, for example **filament lamps with LEDs**.
Using waste heat, for example **combined heat and power** schemes that heat buildings with power-station waste heat.

callouts.p: For full marks, name the method AND explain what it reduces: 'lubricating the axle reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating'.

core.p: Efficient devices need less input energy to do the same useful job. That links efficiency to running costs and to sustainability.
bullets: Less input energy means **lower electricity bills** (fewer kWh paid for).
Less electricity demand means **less fuel burned** in power stations and **lower carbon dioxide emissions**.
Fossil fuel reserves last longer.
An efficient device may cost more to buy, so compare **purchase cost** with **running cost** over its lifetime (payback time).
This is why efficiency appears in the Sustainable energy chapter.

core.p: Many 4 and 6 mark questions give data for two devices and ask which is better. Calculate efficiencies, then use them in a reasoned judgement.
bullets: Calculate the efficiency of **each** device, showing working.
State which is **more efficient** and by how much.
Compare **useful output** for the same input, or input needed for the same useful output.
Bring in **cost**, **lifetime** and **environmental** effects if the data gives them.
Finish with a clear conclusion that answers the question.

callouts.p: Six-mark answers that quote numbers from the table and calculate something always score higher than general statements.

analogy.t: Pocket money and a leaky purse
analogy.p: Imagine you are given 10 pounds (input energy) to spend on books (useful output). On the way to the shop some coins fall through a hole in your purse (wasted energy). The coins are not destroyed: they are still somewhere on the pavement (dissipated into the surroundings), but you cannot use them for books. Efficiency is the fraction of your money that actually buys books. Fixing the hole (lubricating, insulating, streamlining) raises efficiency. Where it breaks down: dropped coins could be picked up again, but dissipated energy is spread so thinly that it is almost impossible to collect and reuse, and money is not a physical quantity that is conserved by a law of nature.

terms.d: The ratio of useful energy transferred to total energy transferred (or useful power output to total power input); no units.
Efficiency multiplied by 100%, giving a value between 0% and 100%.
Energy transferred to the store or by the pathway that is wanted.
Energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
The total energy supplied to a device; equal to useful plus wasted output energy.
The spreading out of energy into the surroundings so that it becomes less useful.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores, so total output equals input.
An energy flow diagram in which arrow widths are proportional to the amounts of energy transferred.
The energy represented by one square or one unit of width on a Sankey diagram.
The rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W); 1 W = 1 J/s.
The energy store associated with the temperature of an object or the surroundings.
A force opposing motion between surfaces that transfers energy to thermal stores, reducing efficiency.
Using oil or grease between moving parts to reduce friction and so reduce wasted energy.
Shaping an object to reduce air resistance and so reduce energy dissipated to the air.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = total energy / useful energy
mistakes.r: Efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy transferred; the answer must be less than 1.

mistakes.w: The wasted energy is lost / destroyed.
mistakes.r: The wasted energy is dissipated (spread out) to the surroundings, usually by heating; it is not destroyed.

mistakes.w: Giving efficiency in joules or watts.
mistakes.r: Efficiency has no units; give a decimal or a percentage.

mistakes.w: Efficiency of 150%.
mistakes.r: Efficiency can never exceed 100% because energy cannot be created; the division was the wrong way round.

mistakes.w: Using wasted energy / input energy as the efficiency.
mistakes.r: Use the USEFUL energy on top; wasted / input gives the fraction wasted.

mistakes.w: The longer arrow on the Sankey diagram has more energy.
mistakes.r: The WIDTH of the arrow is proportional to the energy, not its length.

mistakes.w: Rearranging with a percentage: useful = 40 x 200 = 8000 J.
mistakes.r: Convert 40% to 0.40 first: useful = 0.40 x 200 = 80 J.

mistakes.w: Lubrication makes the machine use less energy.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating and more of the input is transferred usefully.

mistakes.w: Sankey output arrows do not add up to the input.
mistakes.r: Total width of output arrows must equal width of the input arrow (conservation of energy).

exam.q: State the equation that links efficiency, useful energy transferred and total energy transferred.
model: efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy transferred
exam.tip: Write it in words exactly; you may add x 100% for percentage.

exam.q: A lamp is supplied with 200 J of electrical energy and transfers 30 J as light. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
exam.tip: Show the division; the second mark is for converting to a percentage.

exam.q: A motor has an input power of 500 W and an efficiency of 0.8. Calculate the useful power output.
model: useful power = efficiency x input power = 0.8 x 500

exam.q: An electric drill has a useful output of 360 J and is 60% efficient. Calculate the total energy supplied.
model: total = useful / efficiency

exam.q: Explain why the efficiency of a device can never be greater than 100%.
model: Energy cannot be created (conservation of energy)
so useful output cannot be more than input; some energy is always dissipated (e.g. by heating)
exam.tip: Mention conservation of energy by name.

exam.q: State what the width of an arrow on a Sankey diagram represents.
model: The amount of energy transferred (width is proportional to energy)

exam.q: On a Sankey diagram for a TV, the input arrow is 20 squares wide and the light and sound arrows together are 6 squares wide. Each square represents 5 J. Calculate the wasted energy and the efficiency.
model: Wasted = 20 - 6 = 14 squares = 14 x 5 = 70 J
Efficiency = 6 / 20
exam.tip: The scale cancels when finding efficiency.

exam.q: Describe two ways of increasing the efficiency of a bicycle and explain how each works.
model: Lubricate the chain/axles
reduces friction so less energy is dissipated by heating
Streamlined riding position / clothing
reduces air resistance so less energy transferred to the air
exam.tip: Each method needs a matching explanation mark.

exam.q: A filament lamp (10% efficient) and an LED lamp (80% efficient) give the same light output of 8 J each second. Calculate the input power of each lamp and explain why replacing filament lamps reduces carbon dioxide emissions.
model: Filament input = 8 / 0.10 = 80 W
LED input = 8 / 0.80 = 10 W
LED needs less electrical energy for the same light
so less fuel burned in power stations, less CO2 released
exam.tip: Use useful power / efficiency for each lamp.

exam.q: A company must choose between two electric motors. Motor A: input 2000 W, useful output 1500 W, cost 200 pounds. Motor B: input 2000 W, useful output 1800 W, cost 320 pounds. Evaluate which motor the company should buy.
model: Efficiency A = 1500 / 2000 = 75%
Efficiency B = 1800 / 2000 = 90%
B wastes 200 W, A wastes 500 W, so A dissipates more energy by heating
B gives more useful output for the same input, so lower running cost per useful job
A is cheaper to buy (120 pounds less)
Conclusion: B better if used often/long term as running savings outweigh extra cost; A if used rarely
exam.tip: Level-of-response marking: calculate both efficiencies, weigh cost against savings, then give a justified conclusion.

worked.q: A kettle is supplied with 240 000 J of electrical energy. 204 000 J heats the water. Calculate the efficiency and the wasted energy.
steps: Write the equation: efficiency = useful energy / total energy
worked.ans: Efficiency = 0.85 (85%); wasted energy = 36 000 J, which heats the kettle and the surrounding air.

worked.q: A crane motor is 40% efficient. It must transfer 12 kJ to the gravitational store of a load. How much electrical energy must be supplied?
steps: Rearrange: total energy = useful energy / efficiency
worked.ans: 30 000 J (30 kJ) must be supplied; 18 kJ is dissipated.

worked.q: A Sankey diagram uses 1 square = 50 J. The input arrow is 16 squares wide; the useful kinetic arrow is 4 squares wide; the rest is wasted as heating and sound. Find the energies and efficiency.
worked.ans: Input 800 J, useful 200 J, wasted 600 J, efficiency 25%.

phy_ocrb.1.3.summary: Energy resources are the stores we draw on to generate electricity, heat buildings and power transport. They split into **non-renewable** resources (fossil fuels and nuclear fuel), which will eventually run out, and **renewable** resources (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tides, waves, biofuel and geothermal), which are replenished naturally. Most power stations work the same way: something makes a **turbine** spin, the turbine turns a **generator**, and the generator transfers energy electrically to the National Grid. Choosing between resources means weighing reliability, cost, emissions and environmental impact.

core.p: An energy resource is a store of energy that people can use. We use resources for three main jobs: generating electricity, heating, and transport.
bullets: **Primary energy resources** are found in nature: coal, oil, gas, uranium, wind, sunlight, moving water, biomass.
Electricity is a **secondary** source: it is generated from a primary resource and is a convenient way to transfer energy to homes and industry.
Transport mainly uses **oil** products (petrol, diesel, kerosene), with growing use of electricity and biofuels.
Heating mainly uses **natural gas** in the UK, plus electricity, oil and biomass.

callouts.p: The main fuels are fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas), nuclear fuel and biofuel.

core.p: The key difference is whether the resource is replaced as fast as we use it.
bullets: **Non-renewable**: formed over millions of years or present in limited amounts, so once used it is gone. Coal, oil, natural gas, uranium (nuclear).
**Renewable**: replenished naturally on a human timescale. Wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, biofuel, geothermal.
Renewable does not automatically mean reliable or harmless: wind and solar vary, and dams flood valleys.
Biofuel is renewable because new crops can be grown, but it still releases carbon dioxide when burned.

callouts.p: A resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used, so it will not run out.
A resource that is being used up faster than it is replaced, so it will eventually run out.

core.p: Coal, oil and natural gas formed from the remains of plants and sea creatures buried and compressed over millions of years. Burning them transfers energy from their chemical store.
bullets: **Advantages**: reliable, can be switched on to meet demand, relatively cheap, high energy density, existing infrastructure.
Gas power stations have the **shortest start-up time**, so they are used to meet sudden peaks in demand.
**Disadvantages**: release **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that contributes to **climate change**.
Coal and oil release **sulfur dioxide**, causing **acid rain**; burning also releases particulates.
They are non-renewable and will run out; extraction can damage landscapes and oil spills harm wildlife.

callouts.p: Write 'carbon dioxide causes global warming / climate change' and 'sulfur dioxide causes acid rain'. Do not mix them up, and do not say fossil fuels damage the ozone layer.

core.p: Nuclear power stations use **uranium** (or plutonium). **Nuclear fission** of uranium nuclei releases energy that heats water to make steam.
bullets: **Advantages**: no carbon dioxide released during generation, very large energy from a small mass of fuel, reliable baseload supply.
**Disadvantages**: produces **radioactive waste** that stays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored securely.
Risk of accidents releasing radioactive material.
Very high building and **decommissioning** costs; long start-up time, so not used to meet sudden demand.
Uranium is non-renewable.

core.h: How a thermal power station generates electricity
core.p: Fossil fuel, nuclear, biofuel and geothermal stations all heat water to make steam. The steam drives the same chain of equipment.
bullets: 1. Fuel is burned (or nuclear fission happens) to release energy.
2. Energy heats water in a **boiler** to make high-pressure **steam**.
3. Steam pushes on the blades of a **turbine**, making it spin.
4. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which spins and generates a potential difference.
5. Steam is cooled in a **condenser** and the water is reused; waste energy is dissipated to the surroundings (cooling towers).
Energy pathway: chemical (or nuclear) store, then thermal store of steam, then kinetic store of turbine, then electrically to the Grid.

callouts.p: For 'describe how electricity is generated', use the sequence fuel, boiler, steam, turbine, generator, Grid, with one linking word per step.

core.p: A generator turns kinetic energy into an electrical output. Inside, a magnet (or coil) is rotated so that a coil of wire experiences a changing magnetic field.
bullets: When a magnet rotates near a coil, a **potential difference is induced** across the coil.
If the coil is part of a complete circuit, an **electric current** flows.
As the magnet keeps turning, the direction of the p.d. keeps reversing, so power stations produce **alternating current (a.c.)**.
A faster rotation, a stronger magnet or more turns on the coil gives a bigger induced p.d.

callouts.p: Every method except solar cells uses a turning generator. Solar cells transfer energy from light directly to an electrical output.

core.h: Wind, hydroelectric, tidal and wave power
core.p: These renewables use moving air or water to turn a turbine directly, so there is no fuel to burn and no steam.
bullets: **Wind**: moving air turns the blades; no fuel cost, no CO2 when running. But output depends on wind speed, turbines can be noisy and change the look of the landscape.
**Hydroelectric**: water stored behind a dam falls through turbines (gravitational store to kinetic). Reliable and can be started quickly, but flooding valleys destroys habitats and homes.
**Pumped storage** hydro stations pump water uphill when demand is low and release it when demand is high.
**Tidal**: barrages trap water at high tide and release it through turbines. Tides are predictable, but barrages affect estuary habitats and shipping.
**Wave**: floating devices move up and down with waves to drive generators. Unreliable, small output, can be damaged in storms.

core.p: Energy from the Sun can be used in two ways: solar cells for electricity and solar thermal panels for heating water.
bullets: **Solar cells (photovoltaic)** transfer energy from light directly to an electrical output, with no moving parts.
**Solar heating panels** absorb radiation to heat water for homes.
Advantages: no fuel cost, no emissions while running, good for remote places.
Disadvantages: no output at night, less on cloudy days and in winter; large areas needed for big outputs; high initial cost.

core.p: Biofuels are fuels made from plants or animal waste, such as wood, ethanol from sugar cane, or methane from rotting waste.
bullets: Biofuel is **renewable** because crops can be regrown.
It is often described as **carbon neutral**: plants absorb CO2 as they grow, roughly balancing what is released when burned.
Disadvantages: land used for fuel crops cannot grow food; forests may be cleared; CO2 is still released when burned.
**Geothermal**: hot rocks underground heat water to steam, used to drive turbines or heat buildings. Reliable, but only practical in volcanic areas such as Iceland.

callouts.t: Carbon neutral is not zero emission
callouts.p: Burning biofuel DOES release carbon dioxide. It is called carbon neutral only because the growing plants took in a similar amount.

core.p: Exam questions often give a table of data and ask you to evaluate. Use these criteria to structure your answer.
bullets: **Reliability**: can it supply electricity whenever needed?
**Start-up time**: how quickly can it respond to demand?
**Environmental impact**: CO2, other pollutants, waste, habitat damage, visual and noise pollution.
**Cost**: building, fuel, running and decommissioning.
**Sustainability**: will the resource run out?

core.h: Reliability and the need for a mix
core.p: Electricity demand changes through the day and year, but many renewables cannot be switched on when needed. That is why the UK uses a mix of resources.
bullets: **Baseload** demand (always present) is met by steady sources such as nuclear.
**Peaks** in demand are met by quick-start sources: gas and pumped storage hydroelectric.
Wind and solar vary with weather, so backup capacity or energy storage is needed.
A **mix** reduces dependence on any one fuel and on imports.

callouts.p: Do not just say 'wind is unreliable'. Say 'wind turbines produce no electricity when the wind speed is too low, so another source is needed to meet demand'.

core.p: Choosing energy resources involves more than physics. Scientists provide data, but decisions also depend on economics, politics, ethics and local opinion.
bullets: People may support wind power in general but object to a wind farm near their home.
Governments must balance cost, security of supply and climate targets.
There are **risks and benefits** to every option; good answers weigh both sides.
Answers should use evidence (data from the question) to justify a conclusion.

analogy.t: A bank account versus a salary
analogy.p: Non-renewable resources are like savings in a bank account built up over a very long time: you can spend them whenever you like, but once spent they are gone. Renewable resources are like a monthly salary: it keeps coming, but you only get what arrives, and some months (calm or cloudy weather) it is smaller. A sensible person uses both: the salary for everyday spending and savings to cover gaps. Where it breaks down: you can top up a bank account, but fossil fuels take millions of years to form, and the 'salary' from wind or sun cannot be banked easily without large storage systems.

terms.d: A store of energy that can be used by people for electricity, heating or transport.
A resource that is replenished naturally as it is used, so it will not run out.
A resource that will run out because it is used faster than it is replaced.
Coal, oil or natural gas, formed from remains of living things over millions of years.
Uranium or plutonium, whose nuclei undergo fission to release energy.
Splitting of a large nucleus into smaller nuclei, releasing energy.
A fuel made from plant matter or animal waste, such as wood, ethanol or methane.
Releasing about as much carbon dioxide as was absorbed when the fuel was produced.
A set of blades turned by steam, wind or water, connected to a generator.
A device in which a rotating magnet and coil induce a potential difference.
Electricity generated by water from a reservoir falling through turbines.
Hydroelectric scheme that pumps water uphill at low demand to release at peak demand.
A device that transfers energy from light directly to an electrical output.
Energy from hot rocks underground used to heat water or make steam.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to global warming.
Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels.
The time a power station needs to begin supplying electricity after being switched on.

mistakes.w: Renewable resources do not cause any pollution.
mistakes.r: They release no CO2 when generating, but can cause visual, noise or habitat damage, and biofuels release CO2 when burned.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power produces carbon dioxide that causes global warming.
mistakes.r: Nuclear generation releases no CO2; its main problem is long-lived radioactive waste.

mistakes.w: Fossil fuels damage the ozone layer.
mistakes.r: Burning fossil fuels releases CO2 (global warming) and sulfur dioxide (acid rain).

mistakes.w: Wind power is unreliable.
mistakes.r: Wind turbines produce no electricity when the wind is too slow or too fast, so output cannot be controlled to match demand.

mistakes.w: Electricity is an energy resource.
mistakes.r: Electricity is generated from energy resources; it is a way of transferring energy.

mistakes.w: The turbine produces electricity.
mistakes.r: The turbine turns the generator; the generator induces the potential difference.

mistakes.w: Biofuels are renewable so they produce no carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: Biofuels release CO2 when burned; they are carbon neutral because plants absorbed CO2 as they grew.

mistakes.w: Solar cells use steam to turn a turbine.
mistakes.r: Solar cells transfer energy from light directly to an electrical output with no turbine.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power stations can be switched on quickly to meet demand.
mistakes.r: Nuclear stations have long start-up times; gas and pumped storage are used for sudden demand.

worked.q: Model answer: describe the energy transfers in a gas-fired power station.
steps: Natural gas is burned, transferring energy from its chemical store.
This heats water in the boiler, increasing the thermal store of the water and turning it to steam.
High-pressure steam pushes on turbine blades, increasing the kinetic store of the turbine.
The turbine turns the generator, inducing a potential difference so energy is transferred electrically.
Much energy is dissipated by heating the surroundings, e.g. in cooling towers.
worked.ans: Chemical store of gas, then thermal store of water/steam, then kinetic store of turbine and generator, then electrical transfer to the Grid, with waste heating of the surroundings.

worked.q: Applied example: a remote Scottish island with frequent strong winds and no gas supply needs electricity. Recommend a resource.
steps: Identify needs: remote, no fuel pipeline, windy.
Wind turbines suit the windy climate, need no fuel deliveries and release no CO2 when generating.
Wind is variable, so add battery storage or a small diesel backup for calm days.
Wave or tidal schemes may also be possible around the coast.
worked.ans: Wind turbines with storage or backup generation, because the resource is plentiful locally and avoids importing fuel.

worked.q: Model answer: compare nuclear and coal for meeting baseload demand.
steps: Both are reliable and can run continuously, so both suit baseload.
Coal releases large amounts of CO2 and SO2; nuclear releases no CO2 when generating.
Nuclear produces long-lived radioactive waste; coal produces ash.
Both are non-renewable; nuclear has very high build and decommissioning costs.
worked.ans: Nuclear is better for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but its waste and cost are serious drawbacks; coal is cheaper to build but highly polluting.

phy_ocrb.1.4.summary: Mains electricity in the UK is an **alternating current (a.c.)** supply at about **230 V** and **50 Hz**, whereas cells and batteries supply **direct current (d.c.)**. Electricity reaches homes through the **National Grid**, which uses **step-up transformers** to transmit at very high potential difference and low current, cutting energy wasted by heating the cables, and **step-down transformers** to bring it back to a safe 230 V. In homes, three-core cable has **live**, **neutral** and **earth** wires, each with a specific job and colour, and the earth wire and fuse together protect people from electric shock.

core.p: Current can flow in one direction all the time, or keep reversing. The difference comes from how the potential difference (p.d.) of the supply behaves.
bullets: **Direct current (d.c.)**: charges flow in **one direction only**; the p.d. has a constant sign.
Cells, batteries and solar cells supply d.c.
**Alternating current (a.c.)**: the current **repeatedly reverses direction**, because the p.d. keeps changing between positive and negative.
Mains electricity and power-station generators supply a.c., because the rotating magnet in a generator keeps reversing the induced p.d.
On a p.d.-time graph, d.c. is a **horizontal straight line** and a.c. is a **wave** crossing the time axis.

callouts.p: A current that repeatedly reverses its direction.
A current that always flows in the same direction.

fig.cap: Potential difference against time. The blue a.c. trace repeatedly changes between positive and negative values; the red d.c. trace from a battery stays at one constant value.

core.p: You must know the UK mains values and what they mean.
bullets: Mains p.d. is about **230 V**.
Mains frequency is **50 Hz**: the current completes 50 full cycles (changes direction 100 times) every second.
Frequency is measured in **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
230 V is high enough to cause a fatal electric shock, which is why mains safety features matter.

callouts.p: UK mains: a.c., about 230 V, 50 Hz.

core.p: The National Grid is the network of power stations, transformers, pylons and cables that connects electricity generators to consumers across the country.
bullets: It lets electricity generated anywhere be used anywhere in the country.
Power stations can be switched on or off to match changes in **demand**.
It links many different energy resources into one supply.
Main parts: **power stations**, **step-up transformers**, **transmission cables** (overhead on pylons or underground), **step-down transformers**, **consumers**.

callouts.p: A nationwide network of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers.

core.p: This is the most-tested idea in this point. Transmitting at a very high p.d. makes the current small, and a small current wastes much less energy heating the cables.
bullets: Power transmitted = p.d. x current (P = V x I).
For the same power, **increasing V decreases I** by the same factor.
Current in a cable heats it because the cable has **resistance**: power wasted = I squared x R.
Halving the current cuts heating losses to **one quarter**; reducing current by 10 times cuts losses to one hundredth.
Less energy dissipated means the Grid is **more efficient**, saving fuel and money and reducing emissions.
Thinner, cheaper cables can also be used when the current is small.

callouts.p: High p.d., so low current, so less heating of the cables, so less energy wasted, so more efficient. Each link earns a mark.
High voltage does not make electricity travel faster or further. It reduces the current and so reduces energy wasted by heating.

core.p: A transformer changes the size of an alternating p.d. It has two coils of insulated wire wound on an iron core.
bullets: The **primary coil** is connected to the input a.c. supply.
The **secondary coil** gives the output p.d.
A **step-up** transformer has **more turns on the secondary** coil, so output p.d. is greater than input.
A **step-down** transformer has **fewer turns on the secondary** coil, so output p.d. is less than input.
The alternating current in the primary produces a **changing magnetic field** in the iron core, which induces an alternating p.d. in the secondary.
Transformers only work with **a.c.**: a steady d.c. gives no changing magnetic field, so no p.d. is induced.
Transformers are very efficient, often close to 100%.

callouts.p: Transformers need alternating current, so the Grid uses a.c. to allow the p.d. to be stepped up and down.

core.p: Two equations link the input and output of an ideal (100% efficient) transformer. The power equation is the one most often used in Grid questions; the turns-ratio equation explains how the coils set the output p.d.
bullets: **Turns ratio**: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns (p = primary, s = secondary, N = number of turns).
**Power**: for a 100% efficient transformer, power in = power out, so Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.
If the p.d. is stepped up by a factor, the current is stepped **down** by the same factor.
Units: V in volts, I in amperes, N has no unit.
Example: 230 V to 11.5 V with 2000 primary turns gives Ns = 2000 x 11.5 / 230 = 100 turns.

callouts.p: Write the primary values on top and the secondary values underneath in the turns-ratio equation, then cross-multiply.

core.h: Step-up and step-down in the Grid
core.p: Each type of transformer has a specific place in the Grid.
bullets: **Step-up** at the power station: raises p.d. (for example from about 25 kV to as much as 400 kV) for transmission.
**Step-down** at substations near towns: lowers p.d. in stages to 230 V for homes.
Some industry takes electricity at higher p.d. (for example 11 kV or 33 kV).
High p.d. in homes would be far too dangerous, which is why step-down is essential.

core.h: Three-core cable: live, neutral and earth
core.p: Most mains appliances connect with a three-core cable. Each wire is colour-coded and has a different job.
bullets: **Live wire (brown)**: carries the alternating p.d. from the supply, about **230 V**. It is the dangerous wire.
**Neutral wire (blue)**: completes the circuit; it is at or close to **0 V**.
**Earth wire (green and yellow stripes)**: a **safety wire** at 0 V, connected to the metal case of the appliance and to the ground. It only carries current if there is a fault.
Each wire is copper (good conductor) covered in plastic insulation.
The plug casing is plastic or rubber, which are electrical insulators; the pins are brass, which conducts and is hard-wearing.

core.h: Why the live wire is dangerous
core.p: Your body is at 0 V, about the same as earth. Touching the live wire puts a large p.d. across your body.
bullets: A p.d. of about 230 V between live and you drives a **current through your body** to earth.
This can cause an **electric shock**, burns, or stop the heart.
This can happen even when a switch is off if the live wire is touched directly, since the live wire may still be at a high p.d.
A connection between live and earth (for example through a person or metal case) is very dangerous.
Switches and fuses are placed in the **live** wire, so that turning off disconnects the high p.d. from the appliance.

callouts.p: A live wire can be dangerous even if the switch is open, because it is still at a high potential compared with earth.

core.h: How the earth wire and fuse protect you
core.p: If a fault makes the live wire touch a metal case, the earth wire and fuse work together to make the appliance safe.
bullets: The earth wire connects the metal case to the ground, a **low-resistance path**.
If live touches the case, a **very large current** flows from live through the earth wire.
This large current **melts the fuse** (or trips the circuit breaker), breaking the circuit and disconnecting the live wire.
The case is then no longer at a high p.d., so touching it will not give a shock.
Fuse rating should be just above the normal working current (common ratings 3 A, 5 A, 13 A).

callouts.p: Fault, large current through earth wire, fuse melts, circuit broken, case safe. Exams reward this sequence.

core.p: Some appliances, such as hairdryers, have plastic cases and no earth wire. They are double insulated.
bullets: The case is an **insulator**, so it cannot become live even if a wire comes loose.
Two-core cable (live and neutral only) can then be used.
Marked with a symbol of a square inside a square.

analogy.t: Water pipes and a delivery lorry
analogy.p: Think of transmitting electricity like sending water through a long leaky hose. Pushing a huge flow (large current) at low pressure loses lots of water through friction and leaks, but sending a small flow at very high pressure delivers the same amount of water each second with far less loss. Transformers are like pressure changers at each end. The live wire is like a high-pressure pipe: touch it and water bursts through you; the earth wire is an emergency drain that takes the flood away and trips a valve (the fuse). Where it breaks down: electrical current is not a substance that is used up, a.c. charges just move back and forth rather than flowing along, and heating losses depend on current squared, which has no simple water equivalent.

terms.d: Current that always flows in the same direction, as from a cell or battery.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction, as from the mains.
Number of complete cycles per second, in hertz; UK mains is 50 Hz.
The UK domestic supply potential difference, about 230 V.
Network of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Device with two coils on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating p.d.
Transformer with more secondary than primary turns, increasing p.d. and decreasing current.
Transformer with fewer secondary than primary turns, decreasing p.d. and increasing current.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil of a transformer, in which a p.d. is induced.
Brown wire carrying the alternating supply p.d. of about 230 V.
Blue wire completing the circuit, at or near 0 V.
Green and yellow safety wire at 0 V that carries current only if there is a fault.
A thin wire in the live line that melts if the current is too large, breaking the circuit.
Appliance design with an insulating case so no earth wire is needed.
Energy per second dissipated by heating, equal to I squared x R.

mistakes.w: The Grid uses high voltage so electricity travels faster.
mistakes.r: High p.d. gives a low current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.

mistakes.w: High voltage reduces the resistance of the cables.
mistakes.r: Resistance is unchanged; the current is reduced, so I squared R heating is reduced.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power.
mistakes.r: It increases the p.d. and decreases the current; power stays the same (or falls slightly).

mistakes.w: Transformers work with d.c.
mistakes.r: Transformers only work with a.c., because a changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d.

mistakes.w: The neutral wire is the safety wire.
mistakes.r: The earth wire is the safety wire; the neutral completes the circuit.

mistakes.w: The earth wire carries current all the time.
mistakes.r: The earth wire only carries current if there is a fault.

mistakes.w: Live wire is blue / neutral is brown.
mistakes.r: Live is brown, neutral is blue, earth is green and yellow.

mistakes.w: The fuse protects the person by stopping current flowing through them.
mistakes.r: A large fault current through the earth wire melts the fuse, disconnecting the live supply so the case is no longer live.

mistakes.w: Mains is 240 V d.c. at 60 Hz.
mistakes.r: UK mains is a.c., about 230 V, 50 Hz.

exam.q: State the frequency and potential difference of the UK mains supply.
model: 50 Hz
about 230 V

exam.q: Describe the difference between direct current and alternating current.
model: d.c. flows in one direction only
a.c. repeatedly reverses direction

exam.q: State the colour of the earth wire.
model: Green and yellow (stripes)

exam.q: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at very high potential difference.
model: High p.d. means a low current for the same power
lower current means less heating of the cables (less I squared R)
so less energy is wasted / transmission is more efficient
exam.tip: Mention current; this is the key link.

exam.q: Explain why a transformer will not work with a d.c. supply.
model: d.c. produces a constant / unchanging magnetic field in the core
no changing field so no p.d. induced in the secondary coil

exam.q: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 25 turns on the secondary coil. The input p.d. is 230 V. Calculate the output p.d.
model: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
exam.tip: Fewer secondary turns: step-down, so answer should be smaller.

exam.q: A 100% efficient transformer has input 230 V, 2.0 A. Its output p.d. is 11.5 V. Calculate the output current.
model: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
Is = 40 A

exam.q: Explain why touching the live wire can cause an electric shock even when the appliance is switched off.
model: Live wire is still at a high p.d. (about 230 V) relative to earth / your body is at 0 V
so a current would flow through your body to earth
exam.tip: Talk about p.d. between live and you.

exam.q: A kettle has a metal case. Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect the user if the live wire touches the case.
model: Earth wire connects case to ground / low-resistance path
large current flows from live through earth wire
fuse melts (circuit breaker trips)
breaking circuit / disconnecting live so case is not live and user safe

exam.q: Describe how electricity generated at a power station reaches a home, and explain the role of each type of transformer and why a.c. is used.
model: Generator produces a.c. at around 25 kV
Step-up transformer increases p.d. (to e.g. 400 kV)
so current is reduced, reducing heating losses in transmission cables
Electricity transmitted through cables on pylons / National Grid
Step-down transformer at substation reduces p.d. to 230 V, safe for homes
a.c. used because transformers only work with a.c. (changing magnetic field)
exam.tip: Level-of-response: describe the route, explain step-up and step-down, and link a.c. to transformers.

worked.q: A power station delivers 1 000 000 W. Compare the current in the cables if it transmits at 25 000 V or at 400 000 V.
steps: Use P = V x I, so I = P / V.
Current is 16 times smaller at the higher p.d.
Heating loss is I squared R, so losses are 16 x 16 = 256 times smaller.
worked.ans: 40 A at 25 kV versus 2.5 A at 400 kV; transmitting at 400 kV cuts cable heating losses by a factor of 256.

worked.q: A phone charger transformer steps 230 V down to 5 V. The secondary coil has 40 turns. How many turns are on the primary?
An ideal step-up transformer takes 400 V and 50 A and outputs 20 000 V. Find the output current and state the power.
steps: Input power = Vp x Ip = 400 x 50 = 20 000 W.
worked.ans: Output current 1 A; power 20 000 W (20 kW) in and out.

phy_ocrb.1.5.summary: The way people use energy resources changes over time and differs between countries. In the UK, electricity generation has shifted rapidly away from **coal** towards **natural gas** and **renewables** such as wind and solar, driven by **climate change targets**, cost and new technology, while demand still follows strong **daily and seasonal patterns** that the National Grid must match. Worldwide, total energy use is rising as **population grows** and countries **industrialise**, and most energy still comes from **fossil fuels**. You must be able to read graphs and tables of energy data, describe trends, and explain the reasons and consequences, including the social, economic and environmental issues.

core.p: Patterns in energy use come from the choices of people, businesses and governments. Physics explains what each resource can do, but economic, political and environmental factors decide which ones are used.
bullets: **Population growth** increases total demand.
**Economic development**: as countries industrialise and people become richer, energy use per person rises (cars, heating, appliances).
**Technology**: cheaper wind turbines and solar panels; more efficient appliances such as LED lamps.
**Environmental concern**: carbon dioxide from fossil fuels causes climate change, so governments set emission targets.
**Cost and availability** of fuels, including world gas prices.
**Energy security**: avoiding over-reliance on imported fuels.

callouts.p: Global energy demand is rising, and most of it is still met by fossil fuels, but the share from renewables is increasing.

core.h: UK electricity mix: the long-term trend
core.p: The UK has changed its electricity sources more quickly than almost any other country. Trends can be read from data in exam questions; the numbers below are approximate.
bullets: Around 1990 most UK electricity came from **coal**.
In the 1990s many gas-fired power stations were built (the 'dash for gas').
Coal fell sharply after about 2012; the UK's last coal power station closed in **2024**.
**Renewables**, especially offshore and onshore **wind**, rose from a few percent around 2000 to over 40% by the early 2020s.
**Gas** is still a major source and is used to balance supply and demand.
**Nuclear** has supplied a fairly steady share (roughly 15 to 20%) but older stations are closing.

callouts.p: When a graph shows a trend, first DESCRIBE it with numbers from the graph (coal fell from about 40% to under 5%), then EXPLAIN why.

core.h: Reasons for the decline of coal
core.p: Coal produces more carbon dioxide per unit of electricity than any other major fuel, so it was the first target in cutting emissions.
bullets: Burning coal releases large amounts of **CO2** (climate change) and **sulfur dioxide** (acid rain).
UK law (the **Climate Change Act**) set legally binding targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions, now to **net zero by 2050**.
A **carbon price** made coal electricity more expensive.
Gas stations release roughly half the CO2 of coal for the same electricity and start up faster.
UK coal mines closed, so coal would have to be imported.

core.h: Reasons for the growth of renewables
core.p: Wind and solar have grown because they release no carbon dioxide when generating and have become much cheaper.
bullets: The UK is one of the **windiest** countries in Europe, with shallow seas good for **offshore wind farms**.
Cost of wind turbines and solar panels has fallen greatly.
**Government subsidies** and contracts guaranteed prices to encourage investment.
Renewables help meet emission targets and reduce dependence on imported fuel.
Limitation: output depends on weather, so backup (gas, storage, interconnectors) is still needed.

callouts.p: Renewables have grown fast but the UK still uses fossil fuels for much of its heating (gas boilers) and transport (petrol and diesel). Electricity is only part of total energy use.

core.p: Total energy use includes heating and transport as well as electricity. These are much harder to decarbonise.
bullets: Most UK homes are heated by **natural gas** boilers.
Most vehicles still burn **petrol or diesel**.
Switching to **electric vehicles** and **heat pumps** moves this demand onto electricity, which will increase electricity demand in future.
So even as the electricity mix becomes cleaner, total fossil fuel use falls more slowly.

core.p: Electricity demand changes throughout the day, and the Grid must supply exactly what is used at every moment.
bullets: Demand is **lowest at night**, when most people are asleep.
Demand rises in the **morning** as people wake, cook and travel, and as businesses open.
The **peak** is usually in the early **evening** (around 5 to 7 pm), when people cook, use lighting and heating, and watch TV.
Short **surges** happen, for example when many kettles are switched on at the end of a popular TV programme.
Power stations with **short start-up times** (gas, pumped storage hydroelectric) are used to meet peaks.

callouts.p: Electricity is hard to store in large amounts, so the Grid must increase or decrease generation to match demand continuously.

core.p: Demand also changes through the year.
bullets: UK demand is **higher in winter**: more lighting (longer nights) and more heating.
Demand is **lower in summer** in the UK, though hot countries have summer peaks from air conditioning.
Solar output is **highest in summer**, when UK demand is lowest; wind output tends to be higher in winter.
Baseload stations (nuclear) run all the time; others are scheduled for times of high demand.

core.p: As more electricity comes from wind and solar, the Grid has to cope with supply that changes with the weather, not just demand that changes with the time of day.
bullets: **Pumped storage** hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill when supply is high or demand low.
**Large batteries** store energy for short periods.
**Interconnectors** (undersea cables) import and export electricity with other countries.
Gas stations provide **flexible backup**.
Smart meters and pricing encourage people to use electricity when supply is high.

core.h: World patterns and differences between countries
core.p: Energy use per person varies hugely between countries. This links to wealth, climate, industry and population.
bullets: **Developed countries** (USA, UK, Europe) use far more energy per person than many developing countries.
**Total** use can be high in countries with large populations even when use per person is lower (for example China and India).
Global energy demand is **rising**, mainly in developing economies as they industrialise.
Most world energy still comes from **fossil fuels** (oil, coal and gas).
Countries use resources they have: hydroelectric in Norway, geothermal in Iceland, nuclear in France, coal in some developing economies.

callouts.p: Always check whether a graph shows total energy use or energy use per person (per capita). They tell different stories.
