core.p: Many questions give a graph, pie chart or table and ask you to describe, calculate or evaluate. Practise reading data accurately.
bullets: Read values carefully, including **units** (TWh, GW, %, kWh per person).
Calculate **changes** and **percentages**: change = new - old; percentage of total = part / total x 100.
Describe trends with words such as **increased**, **decreased**, **peaked**, **levelled off**, and quote values.
Spot **correlations**, for example between GDP per person and energy use, but do not claim cause without a mechanism.
Consider whether the data source is **reliable** and whether the sample of years or countries is enough to support a conclusion.

callouts.p: GW is power (rate); TWh or kWh is energy. A graph of demand in GW shows the rate of use at each moment, not the total energy.

core.p: Predicting future energy use involves uncertainty, so scientists and governments use models and consider different scenarios.
bullets: Demand for electricity is expected to **rise** with electric vehicles and heat pumps.
More **renewable** capacity and **storage** will be needed.
New nuclear stations are being considered for low-carbon baseload.
Improving **efficiency** and **insulation** reduces demand.
Decisions balance **cost**, **reliability**, **environmental impact** and **public opinion**; different people weigh these differently.

core.p: Energy choices affect people unequally, so answers on this point often need you to discuss different viewpoints.
bullets: Burning fossil fuels gives cheap, reliable energy now but **risks** climate change affecting future generations and poorer countries most.
Developing countries argue they should be allowed to use fossil fuels to grow, as rich countries did.
Local people may oppose wind farms, tidal barrages or new nuclear stations near them.
Higher energy prices can cause **fuel poverty**.
A good evaluation gives **both sides** and reaches a supported conclusion.

analogy.p: Think of the world's energy supply like the food bill of a growing family. More children (population growth) and richer tastes (development) mean the bill keeps rising. For years the family relied on cheap takeaways (fossil fuels): convenient, always available, but bad for long-term health (climate). Now they are growing more of their own vegetables (renewables): healthier and free once the garden is planted, but the harvest depends on the weather, so they keep a freezer (storage) and still order takeaway on bad days (gas backup). Meals peak at dinner time, just like the evening peak in demand. Where it breaks down: a family can easily store food for weeks, but storing electricity on a national scale is still difficult and expensive.

terms.d: The combination of different energy resources used to supply a country's energy or electricity.
A general pattern of change in data over time, such as a steady increase.
The amount of electrical power that consumers are using at a given time.
The highest demand in a period, usually early evening in the UK.
The minimum level of demand that is always present, met by steadily running stations.
Time for a power station to begin supplying electricity after being switched on.
Per person; total divided by population.
A country with high income and industry, typically high energy use per person.
A country with lower average income and energy use per person, often growing fast.
Balancing greenhouse gases emitted with those removed, so there is no net addition.
UK law setting legally binding targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Having a reliable, affordable supply of energy without over-dependence on imports.
A cable linking the electricity grids of different countries.
Storing energy by pumping water uphill, releasing it through turbines at high demand.
A link between two variables in data, which does not by itself prove one causes the other.
When a household cannot afford to heat its home adequately.

mistakes.w: Describing a trend with no numbers: 'coal went down'.
mistakes.r: Quote data: 'coal fell from about 40% in 2012 to under 5% by 2018'.

mistakes.w: The UK gets all its energy from renewables now.
mistakes.r: Renewables supply a large share of electricity, but gas is still major and heating and transport mostly use fossil fuels.

mistakes.w: Demand is highest at midday because the Sun is up.
mistakes.r: UK demand peaks in the early evening when people return home and use cooking, lighting and heating.

mistakes.w: Countries with high total energy use must have high use per person.
mistakes.r: Total depends on population too; a country with a huge population can have high total but low per capita use.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power is used for peak demand.
mistakes.r: Nuclear has a long start-up time and is used for baseload; gas and pumped storage meet peaks.

mistakes.w: Coal stopped being used because it ran out.
mistakes.r: Coal was phased out mainly to cut CO2 emissions to meet climate targets and because of carbon pricing and cheaper alternatives.

mistakes.w: Correlation proves that wealth causes energy use.
mistakes.r: Data show a correlation; you need a mechanism (more cars, appliances, industry) to explain a causal link.

mistakes.w: GW on a demand graph is the energy used.
mistakes.r: GW is power (rate of transfer); energy is power x time, e.g. GWh or TWh.

exam.q: State one reason why total world energy demand is increasing.
model: Growing population / countries industrialising / rising standard of living

exam.q: Give two reasons why the use of coal for UK electricity generation has fallen.
model: Burning coal releases large amounts of CO2 / to meet emission targets
Gas / renewables cheaper or cleaner; carbon price; coal mines closed

exam.q: Describe how UK electricity demand changes during a typical winter day.
model: Lowest during the night
rises in the morning
peaks in the early evening (about 5 to 7 pm), then falls
exam.tip: Use the time of day and a describing word for each mark.

exam.q: Explain why UK electricity demand is higher in winter than in summer.
model: Longer hours of darkness so more lighting
colder so more electric heating
exam.tip: Give a reason linked to the season.

exam.q: Suggest why gas-fired power stations are used to meet the evening peak in demand.
model: Short start-up time
so output can be increased quickly as demand rises
exam.tip: Link the property to the need.

exam.q: A country's electricity generation increased from 250 TWh to 320 TWh. Calculate the percentage increase.
model: Increase = 70 TWh; 70 / 250 x 100

exam.q: In one year, wind supplied 82 TWh of a total 290 TWh of UK electricity. Calculate the percentage supplied by wind.
Explain why increasing the share of electricity from wind and solar makes it harder to match supply with demand.
model: Output depends on weather / no solar at night, little wind on calm days
cannot be switched on when demand rises
so backup (gas) or storage (pumped storage, batteries) is needed
exam.tip: Mention a solution for the third mark.

exam.q: Some countries use much more energy per person than others. Suggest two reasons for this.
model: Higher wealth / more cars and appliances / more industry
Colder or hotter climate needs more heating or air conditioning
exam.tip: Give reasons, not just names of countries.

exam.q: A graph shows that the share of UK electricity from renewables rose from 7% in 2010 to 43% in 2020 while coal fell from 28% to 2%. Discuss the reasons for these trends and the issues they create for the future of the UK energy supply.
model: Describe: renewables up by about 36 percentage points, coal down by about 26
Reasons: climate change targets / net zero; CO2 from coal; carbon pricing
Falling costs of wind and solar; UK windy with good offshore sites; subsidies
Issue: renewable output depends on weather, so supply may not match demand
Need storage, backup gas or interconnectors; gas still emits CO2
Future demand rising with electric cars and heat pumps; conclusion weighing reliability, cost and emissions
exam.tip: Level-of-response: describe with data, explain causes, then discuss consequences and reach a view.

worked.q: Table: UK electricity 2010 total 380 TWh with renewables 26 TWh; 2020 total 312 TWh with renewables 134 TWh. Calculate the renewable percentage each year and describe the trend.
steps: Note that total generation fell, partly due to more efficient appliances and lower industrial use.
worked.ans: Renewables rose from about 7% to about 43% of UK electricity between 2010 and 2020, while total generation fell.

worked.q: A demand graph shows 22 GW at 4 am and 40 GW at 6 pm. How much extra power is needed at the peak, and what kind of power stations should supply it?
steps: This extra is needed only for a few hours.
Stations must have short start-up times and flexible output.
Gas-fired stations and pumped storage hydroelectric are suitable; nuclear is not because of its long start-up time.
worked.ans: 18 GW extra, supplied by fast-starting gas and pumped storage stations.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why world energy use is expected to keep rising even though the UK's is falling.
steps: Developing countries are industrialising, so energy use per person is rising there.
The UK's use is falling due to more efficient devices, insulation and less heavy industry.
Falls in some developed countries are smaller than rises elsewhere.
worked.ans: Growth from population and development in developing countries outweighs efficiency savings in countries such as the UK.
